stem: An analyst needs to establish whether a workstation's connection to an external address on port 8443 was permitted or dropped at the perimeter. Which source answers this most directly?

options.text: Firewall logs
options.why: Allow and deny decisions per flow are exactly what a firewall records. The question is about the perimeter's verdict, which only the perimeter holds.

options.text: Endpoint detection logs from the workstation
options.why: EDR shows the process attempted the connection. It does not reliably show whether the firewall let it through.

options.text: OS security logs from the workstation
options.why: Those record logons, privilege use and policy changes, not network decisions made elsewhere.

options.text: Application logs from the destination service
options.why: You do not control the external destination, and if the flow was dropped there is nothing there to log.

stem: An investigation needs to know which account authenticated interactively to a server at 02:14 and whether it used elevated privileges. Which source is designed to answer this?

options.text: The operating system security log on that server
options.why: Logon events, logon types and privilege use are core OS security log content. It is the authoritative record of who signed in and as what.

options.text: Firewall logs for traffic to that server
options.why: A firewall sees a flow to a port. It has no idea which account was used inside that session.

options.text: IDS logs covering the server's segment
options.why: An IDS reports traffic matching a signature or deviating from a baseline. A normal authentication produces neither.

options.text: A vulnerability scan of the server from that week
options.why: A scan lists weaknesses that existed. It records nothing about who logged in.

stem: A finance user's account was used to alter twelve supplier bank details inside the ERP system. The account authenticated normally and no malware was found. Which source best reconstructs exactly what was changed and in what order?

options.text: Application logs from the ERP system
options.why: Only the application knows its own transactions. When the activity is legitimate-looking use of a real account, the layers below see nothing unusual and the application is the entire story.

options.text: OS security logs from the ERP server
options.why: They will confirm a session existed. They cannot name which supplier records were edited.

options.text: Endpoint logs from the user's workstation
options.why: EDR shows processes and files on the endpoint. The changes happened server-side inside the application.

options.text: Packet captures from the finance segment
options.why: The session is almost certainly encrypted, and a capture would only exist if someone had been recording that segment beforehand.

stem: Which source would show that inbound traffic matched a known exploit signature and was dropped before reaching the application?

options.text: IPS logs
options.why: An intrusion prevention system is inline, matches against signatures, and records both the match and the action taken. That combination is unique to it.

options.text: Firewall logs
options.why: A traditional firewall decides on addresses, ports and state. It would have permitted this flow, because the problem was inside the payload.

options.text: Application logs
options.why: If the traffic was dropped before arriving, the application saw nothing and logged nothing.

options.text: Network flow records
options.why: Flow data shows a conversation occurred and how much passed. It carries no signature matching.

stem: A SOC dashboard shows a spike in failed authentications at 03:00 four days ago. The analyst wants the individual attempts: usernames, source addresses and exact times. What should they do?

options.text: Query the raw log data the dashboard is built on
options.why: A dashboard is a view, not a source: it shows an aggregate over a rolling window. Aggregation is what makes it readable and also what removes the per-event detail an investigation needs.

options.text: Export the dashboard panel, which contains the source events
options.why: Exporting a chart gives you the chart. The counts behind a bar are not the events behind the counts.

options.text: Re-run the scheduled automated report covering that day
options.why: A report is another summary. It may confirm the spike and still will not name the accounts.

options.text: Run a vulnerability scan against the affected authentication server
options.why: That describes weaknesses that exist now. It says nothing about what happened four days ago.

stem: During an investigation a team retrieves a vulnerability scan report produced three weeks before the breach. What does this evidence actually establish?

options.text: That the weakness was present and known before the breach
options.why: A scan is a point-in-time statement of what was possible. It speaks to the organization's response rather than to the attacker's actions: powerful for root cause and accountability, and not a record of the event. Scans show exposure; logs show events.

options.text: That the attacker used this specific vulnerability to gain access
options.why: The scan cannot connect a listed weakness to an actual intrusion. That requires logs showing the exploitation.

options.text: The time at which the attacker's compromise of the host began
options.why: A scan has no view of attacker activity, so it cannot bound a timeline.

options.text: Which accounts the attacker used after first gaining access
options.why: That comes from OS security logs and application logs, not from a scan.

stem: An analyst wants to know how much data left the network to a suspicious address over the past month, and when. No packet capture was running. What is the best available source?

options.text: Network flow records for that period
options.why: Flow data is the standard answer for historical 'who talked to whom and how much': endpoints, volume and timing without content. It is small enough to retain for months, which is exactly why it survives when captures do not.

options.text: Retrospective packet capture from the span port
options.why: Captures exist only if they were running at the time. You cannot capture the past.

options.text: Endpoint logs from every workstation in the estate
options.why: Possible in principle and impractical across a month and an estate, and it misses anything without an agent.

options.text: The SOC dashboard's egress traffic panel
options.why: A dashboard will likely not retain a month, and its aggregation hides the per-destination detail.

stem: A process on a workstation wrote a file to a user profile and then established an outbound connection. Which TWO sources together best evidence that sequence? (Choose two.)

options.text: EDR logs tying the process to its file write and connection
options.why: EDR is built to tie a process to its own file and network activity, which is the only place the sequence exists as one story.

options.text: Firewall logs showing whether that connection was permitted
options.why: The endpoint shows the attempt; the firewall shows the verdict. Together they establish both intent and outcome.

options.text: The SOC dashboard's malware panel covering that whole day
options.why: An aggregate view, useful for noticing and useless for reconstructing a single host's sequence.

options.text: Application logs from the organization's ERP system for that user
options.why: Unrelated to this host's process and file activity.

options.text: A vulnerability scan of the workstation taken that same week
options.why: Describes what was possible on the host, not what the process actually did.

stem: Reviewing a suspected intrusion, which THREE findings are indicators of compromise rather than ordinary operations? (Choose three.)

options.text: A 45 minute gap in the security log while the host was running
options.why: A running host generates events. A gap is positive evidence something removed them.

options.text: A signed Microsoft binary loading a DLL from a user's AppData
options.why: Legitimate binaries do not normally load code from a user profile. This is the classic living-off-the-land pattern.

options.text: Outbound connections to one host every 60 seconds for nine days
options.why: Machine-regular timing to a single destination is beaconing, not human browsing.

options.text: A server showing sustained high CPU and slow response times all week
options.why: A symptom of load. It is as likely to be a victim of the incident as a participant in it.

options.text: An antivirus full scan completing with zero detections on the host
options.why: A clean signature scan proves nothing when the technique has no signature. It is not itself an indicator.

stem: Flow records show a workstation sent 2 GB to an external address last night. The analyst now needs to know what was actually inside the unencrypted traffic. Which source can answer that?

options.text: Packet captures covering that period
options.why: Full packet capture keeps the payload, so unencrypted content can be reconstructed. It only exists if capture was running at the time.

options.text: Network flow metadata
options.why: Metadata records who talked to whom, when and how much. It never contains the payload.

options.text: The firewall allow log entry for the session
options.why: A firewall log records that the connection was permitted, with addresses, ports and byte counts. It does not store content.

options.text: The weekly vulnerability scan report
options.why: A scan describes weaknesses on a host at scan time. It holds no record of traffic that left the host.

stem: A server and a file share both appear in an incident timeline. The server has a new service set to autostart and an unknown binary in a temp folder. The file share only had its files encrypted by an account that was stolen elsewhere, and shows no malicious software of its own. How should the two hosts be classified?

options.text: The server is compromised; the file share is affected
options.why: Resident malware and persistence are evidence of compromise. The share only shows the effects of someone else's actions.

options.text: Both are compromised because both appear in the incident
options.why: Appearing in the timeline is not evidence of compromise. Rebuilding hosts with no malicious artefacts wastes effort and hides the real scope.

options.text: Neither is compromised until a vulnerability scan is run
options.why: A scan reports weaknesses, not intrusions. The artefacts already found on the server are the evidence.

options.text: Only the file share is compromised because its data was changed
options.why: Changed data is an effect. The share was the victim; the foothold is on the server.

stem: An analyst needs to know whether a connection from the internet to a web server was permitted or blocked at the network edge, and which rule decided it. Which log answers that most directly?

options.text: Firewall log
options.why: Firewall logs record the allow or deny action and the rule that matched, with source, destination and port.

options.text: Application log on the web server
options.why: The application log only shows requests that reached the application. A blocked connection never gets there.

options.text: Operating system security log on the web server
options.why: OS security logs cover logons and policy events on that host, not the edge rule decision.

options.text: Automated weekly report
options.why: A report is a summary built from underlying logs, produced later, and rarely carries per-connection rule detail.

stem: A dashboard shows authentication failures peaked at 03:00. An investigator must prove which source address was responsible and for which accounts. What is the correct next step?

options.text: Pull the underlying authentication logs for that window
options.why: Dashboards and reports summarise. Per-event evidence such as source address and account comes from the underlying logs.

options.text: Screenshot the dashboard panel and keep it as the evidence
options.why: A chart is derived from data and cannot show individual source addresses or accounts. It is a pointer, not proof.

options.text: Rescan the authentication server for vulnerabilities
options.why: A scan finds weaknesses now. It does not explain what happened at 03:00.

options.text: Treat every host that logged a failure as compromised
options.why: Failed attempts show a host was targeted, not that it was breached.

stem: A user reports an email that appears to come from the finance director. The analyst needs to trace which servers handled the message and judge whether the sender address was forged. Which data source does this?

options.text: Application logs from the user's email client showing when the message was opened
options.why: They show what the user did with the message, not the path it took to arrive.

options.text: The message headers, which are metadata recording the relay path and the sending servers
options.why: Headers record each server that handled the message and the claimed and actual origin, so they are the evidence for spoofing.

options.text: Firewall logs for the mail gateway, which record each connection made to the company's mail servers
options.why: They record connections, not the sender's claimed identity or the full relay path inside the message.

options.text: A vulnerability scan of the mail server, to see whether the sender's mail system is vulnerable
options.why: A scan describes weaknesses in the server. It says nothing about one message.

stem: An IDS log shows an alert for a known exploit sent to a web server at 14:05. The sensor sits passively on a mirror port. The analyst must decide whether the attack reached the server. What does the alert establish?

options.text: That the attack succeeded, because an IDS only raises an alert on traffic that actually reached its target
options.why: A passive sensor sees a copy of the traffic. It alerts on a signature match whether or not the server accepted the request.

options.text: That the attack was blocked, because a signature match always stops the traffic before it reaches the server
options.why: Blocking is what an in-line IPS does. A passive IDS on a mirror port detects and records only.

options.text: That a matching exploit attempt crossed the network; the server's own logs show if it worked
options.why: A detection event is evidence of an attempt. The outcome is shown by the systems that received it. Passive sensor: it saw the attack, it did not stop it.

options.text: Nothing yet, because signature alerts can be ignored until a second sensor has confirmed them
options.why: A signature match is evidence to be followed up, not discarded, and it gives a time and target to search on.

stem: Investigators hold a full packet capture of a suspected exfiltration session. The traffic is TLS encrypted and they do not have the keys. What can they still establish from the capture?

options.text: The endpoints, timing, packet sizes and volume: where, when and how much, not what
options.why: Encryption protects the payload, not the addressing or the pattern of the conversation. Encrypted hides the what, not the who, when or how much.

options.text: The exact files that were sent, by reassembling the packets in the capture back into whole files
options.why: Reassembly recovers only ciphertext without the keys.

options.text: Which user account performed the transfer, from the identity carried in the packets
options.why: Packets carry addresses, not accounts. Identity comes from endpoint, application or authentication logs.

options.text: Nothing at all, because a capture of encrypted traffic cannot be used as evidence
options.why: The capture remains valid evidence of the connection and its size and timing, even though the content is unreadable.

stem: An analyst merges firewall and endpoint logs and finds that the endpoint records a malicious download seven minutes before the firewall allowed that connection, which cannot be true. Both sources are in the same time zone, and every other event the two have in common shows the same seven minute gap. What should be dealt with before drawing any conclusion?

options.text: The firewall's rule log, which should be ignored altogether because its timing is clearly wrong
options.why: Discarding a source on one inconsistency throws away evidence and does not explain it.

options.text: Unsynchronized clocks, so normalize the timestamps to a common source before correlating
options.why: A fixed offset between sources points to clock drift. Correlation depends on consistent time, so it must be corrected for first.

options.text: Tampering with the endpoint log by the attacker, so the endpoint data should be discarded
options.why: Tampering is possible, but a consistent seven minute offset is more simply explained by clocks. Conclusions should wait until the offset is checked.

options.text: A slow download that finished seven minutes after the firewall made its decision
options.why: The stem says the endpoint recorded the event before the firewall allowed the connection, which a slow download cannot explain.

stem: An investigation confirms that an attacker exploited a specific unpatched weakness on one web server. Management asks how far the same weakness extends. What is the most appropriate use of vulnerability scan data?

options.text: Treat the scan results as proof that the other hosts running the same software were also exploited by the attacker
options.why: A scan shows exposure, not exploitation. Finding the same weakness elsewhere makes those hosts at risk, not compromised.

options.text: Use the scan results to show what the attacker actually did on the web server after exploiting it
options.why: A scan describes the state of the system. What was done on it is shown by logs.

options.text: Skip scanning altogether, because only logs have any value in an investigation
options.why: Scan data answers a different question, where else the weakness exists, and is valuable for scoping.

options.text: Rerun scans for every host with the same software to find other exposed systems, then check their logs
options.why: The scan scopes the exposure and the logs establish whether any of it was used. Scans find where else it could happen; logs show where it did.

stem: An investigator is using a SOC dashboard to understand an incident. Which TWO limitations must be allowed for? (Choose two.)

options.text: It cannot be used to notice unusual activity or emerging trends
options.why: Noticing trends and anomalies is exactly what dashboards are good for.

options.text: Its panels are aggregates, so single events must come from the logs
options.why: The panels hide the detail. Evidence about particular events lives in the logs the dashboard is built on.

options.text: It keeps a complete copy of every raw event behind its panels
options.why: Dashboards display the results of queries. They are not the system of record for the raw data.

options.text: It shows only what its queries look for, so a quiet panel proves nothing
options.why: An absent pattern may only mean that no one built a panel for it. Nothing on the screen does not mean nothing happened.

options.text: Its figures can be accepted as the original evidence, without checking logs
options.why: A derived view is not the original evidence, and what it shows has to be traceable to the logs.

stem: An analyst believes an attacker moved from a compromised workstation to a file server over RDP at 01:20. Which TWO sources best evidence that movement? (Choose two.)

options.text: The file server's security log of the remote logon and source
options.why: The receiving system records who logged on, with which account, how and from where. It is the strongest evidence of the movement.

options.text: The vulnerability scan of the file server taken last month
options.why: A scan shows what was possible then, not what happened at 01:20.

options.text: Flow records of the RDP connection between the hosts at 01:20
options.why: An independent record of the connection, with source, destination, port and time, corroborates the host log.

options.text: The SOC dashboard's daily count of logons across all the servers
options.why: A daily total cannot show an individual connection at a particular minute.

options.text: Application logs from the HR system covering the same night
options.why: Unrelated to the movement between these two hosts.

stem: A web application's database returned thousands of customer rows to a single client in one request. The analyst needs the exact malicious input that was submitted. Which source most likely holds it?

options.text: Firewall logs, which record the permitted connection to port 443 along with its payload and parameters
options.why: A firewall logs addresses, ports and the decision. It does not record request content.

options.text: NetFlow records for the web server, which show every request the client made
options.why: Flow records show endpoints and volume, not the contents of a request.

options.text: The database server's OS security logs for the web application's service account logon
options.why: They show that the application connected, which it does legitimately all day. The input is recorded elsewhere.

options.text: Web server and application logs recording the full request, including the query string or form values
options.why: The application is the place that received the input and often logs it, so it holds the exact malicious string.

stem: A file server's shares are being encrypted. The server's EDR shows no malicious process on it, only thousands of file renames over SMB by user account j.harkin from 10.1.4.13. Which action best identifies the compromised host?

options.text: Rebuild the file server first, since all of the visible damage is on it and restoring service matters most to the business
options.why: The server is where the effects appear. Rebuilding it while the encrypting process keeps running elsewhere means the files are damaged again.

options.text: Isolate the host at 10.1.4.13, check its endpoint logs for the encrypting process, reset j.harkin's credentials
options.why: The renames come over SMB from that address, so the process is running there. Credentials are reset because the account is also in the attacker's hands.

options.text: Disable j.harkin's account, and treat the incident as contained once that account is locked and the sessions are closed
options.why: Disabling the account stops this session but leaves the malware on the source host, and the attacker may hold other credentials.

options.text: Investigate the domain controller first, because it authenticated j.harkin and so must be the compromised host here
options.why: A system that authenticated a user is not thereby compromised. The evidence points to the host that is sending the renames.

stem: An investigator needs to know which user ran privileged commands with sudo on a Linux server, and when. Which source holds that?

options.text: The Linux auth log, such as /var/log/auth.log or /var/log/secure
options.why: It records authentication and privilege elevation events with the user and the time. It is the operating system's own security record.

options.text: The Windows Security event log on the domain controller for the network
options.why: That records Windows logons and directory events. A Linux server's sudo use is logged on the Linux host.

options.text: Firewall logs for the subnet where the server sits
options.why: A firewall sees connections between hosts, not commands run locally.

options.text: IDS alerts for the server's IP address over the day
options.why: IDS alerts reflect traffic signatures. Local commands do not cross the network.

stem: Analysis must prove that 3 GB of finance files left a file server at 02:00 for an external address, which files they were, and which process on the server sent them. Which THREE sources together best establish this? (Choose three.)

options.text: A vulnerability scan of the file server from the previous week
options.why: It shows weaknesses that existed, not what was sent.

options.text: Firewall or flow logs showing the outbound volume and destination
options.why: They give the amount, the destination and the time, from a point the compromised server does not control.

options.text: File server access logs showing which files were read just before
options.why: Object access auditing on the server is the record of which files were touched in the minutes before the transfer.

options.text: The SOC dashboard panel showing total outbound traffic for the day
options.why: A daily aggregate cannot attribute 3 GB to one host, file set or process.

options.text: Server endpoint logs showing the sending process and its parent
options.why: Process telemetry ties the transfer to a specific program and how it was started.

stem: An in-line IPS logged 600 blocked exploit attempts against a web server overnight, all from one address. What should the analyst conclude and do next?

options.text: The server is compromised, because 600 attempts from one address prove that at least one succeeded
options.why: Blocked attempts are evidence of targeting, not of success.

options.text: No further work is needed, because a blocked attempt tells the analyst nothing at all about the server
options.why: The activity is worth checking, since attackers vary their approach and one variant may not match a signature.

options.text: Rebuild the server immediately, because it was the target of a sustained attack from outside
options.why: Being the target does not make a host compromised. Rebuilding on this evidence is premature.

options.text: It was targeted and the attempts blocked: affected, not shown compromised; check its logs
options.why: The IPS shows attempts and outcomes at its position. The server's own logs show whether anything got past it. Targeted is not compromised.
